title: Multi-Application Survivable Tether
source:
{{update|date=November 2010}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2020}}
The '''Multi-Application Survivable Tether''' ('''MAST''') experiment was an [[outer space|in-space]] investigation designed to use [[CubeSat]] spacecraft connected by [[Tether satellite|tethers]] to better understand the survivability of tethers in space.<ref name="overview">Robert Hoyt, Jeffrey Slostad, and Robert Twiggs, "[http://www.tethers.com/papers/MASTJPC2003Paper.pdf The Multi-application Survivable Tether (MAST) Experiment] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110517195150/http://www.tethers.com/papers/MASTJPC2003Paper.pdf |date=17 May 2011 }}," paper AIAA-2003-5219 presented at the 39th AIAAA/SME/SAE/ASEE Joint Propulsion Conference and Exhibit, Huntsville AL, July 2003</ref> It was launched as a secondary payload on a [[Dnepr (rocket)|Dnepr rocket]] on 17 April 2007 into a 98°, 647 x 782 km orbit.  The MAST payload incorporated three picosatellites, named "Ralph," "Ted," and "Gadget,"  which were intended to separate and deploy a {{convert|1|km|mi|abbr=on}} tether. The experiment hardware was designed under a NASA Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) collaboration between [[Tethers Unlimited, Inc.|Tethers Unlimited, Inc]]. (TUI) (which is now part of the Arka Corporation)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Our Legacy |url=https://arka.org/our-legacy/ |access-date=2024-01-03 |website=Arka |language=en-US}}</ref> and [[Stanford University]], with TUI developing the tether, tether deployer, tether inspection subsystem, satellite avionics, and software, and Stanford students developing the satellite structures and assisting with the avionics design.<ref>
{{cite web | url = http://www.tethers.com/Missions.html | title = The MAST Experiment | publisher = Tethers Unlimited | url-status = dead | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20061110091605/http://www.tethers.com/Missions.html | archivedate = 10 November 2006}}
</ref>

The experiment is currently on-orbit.{{update after|2011|02|04}} After launch, as of 25 April 2007, TUI had made contact with the "Gadget" picosatellite, but not with "Ted", the tether-deployer picosatellite, or "Ralph," the end mass.<ref>
{{cite web | url = http://www.tethers.com/MAST_Blog.html | title = MAST Blog | publisher = Tethers Unlimited | url-status = dead | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20071008083138/http://www.tethers.com/MAST_Blog.html | archivedate = 8 October 2007}}
</ref>

== Satellites ==
The MAST experiment consists of three [[CubeSats]] (3U) launched together as a stack.<ref name="overview" /> The entire stack was about the size of a loaf of bread.<ref name= "young">Kelly Young, "[https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn11716-no-signal-yet-heard-from-tetherdeploying-satellite.html No signal yet heard from tether-deploying satellite]," ''New Scientist,'' 25 April 2007 (accessed 16 February 2012)</ref>
; Gadget
The middle satellite in the stack, called "Gadget", is the tether inspector. Gadget was designed to slowly crawl up and down the tether after deployment, acquiring images as it moves.<ref name="overview" /> As of 9 May 2007, the MAST team has downloaded over 1 MB of data from Gadget. Gadget's GPS receiver has acquired an almanac from the GPS satellites, but apparently has not yet achieved a trajectory solution.{{update after|2011|02|04}}
; Ted
"Ted", the tether deployer satellite, is at one end of the stack. Researchers were unable to establish contact with Ted,<ref name= "young" /> and remain uncertain of its status.
; Ralph
"Ralph" is at the other end of the stack, and is described as simply a "tether endmass". Its design did include a radio, but the groundstation has not received any signals from Ralph.  They think Ralph's battery charge has dropped below the level needed to sustain radio operation.<ref name= "klofas" />

==Deployment==
The experimenter team made contact with the "Gadget" picosatellite, but not with "Ted", the tether-deployer [[picosatellite]], because the Ted pico satellite was powered only by a primary battery, which had depleted by the time the team gained access to the ground station.<ref name= "young" /> While the system was designed so that the satellites would separate even if communications were not established to the tether deployer, the system did not fully deploy. Radar measurements show the tether initially deployed just 1 meter,<ref name= "klofas">Bryan Klofas, Jason Anderson, and Kyle Leveque, "[http://www.klofas.com/papers/CommSurvey-Bryan_Klofas.pdf A Survey of Cubesat Communications Systems], November 2008 (accessed 16 February 2012).  Analysis of flight data indicated that over a period of a week, an additional 5-10 meters of tether deployed.  The short deployment was traced to a failure of the separation mechanism to eject the "Ted" pico satellite at full velocity. Presented at the CubeSat Developers Conference, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, 10 April 2008</ref><ref>R. Hoyt, N. Voronka, T. Newton, I. Barnes, J. Shepherd, S. Frank, and J. Slostad, "Early Results of the Multi-Application Survivable Tether (MAST) Space Tether Experiment", ''Proceedings of the 21st AIAA/USU [[Small Satellite Conference|Conference on Small Satellites]]'', SCC07-VII-8, August 2007.</ref> The mission experienced communications challenges due to limited availability of the ground station, which resulted in the team establishing contact with only one of the three pico satellites.  The team operated the "Gadget" picosatellite for nearly two months before terminating the experiment.
